movement: Step from a chord tone, then a step in the same direction to a chord tone. Accented or not accented
effect_or_use: Connects two chord tones. Two in sequence are double passing tones

movement: Step away from a chord tone, then a step back to the same tone
effect_or_use: Decorates one note. An upper form and a lower form

movement: Step from a chord tone, then a leap in the opposite direction
effect_or_use: An incomplete neighbour tone. Not accented

movement: A note of the subsequent chord comes early
effect_or_use: Not accented. It makes the arrival softer

movement: A note stays from the chord before, then goes down one step
effect_or_use: Accented. The dissonance is on the strong beat. A suspension that goes up is a retardation

movement: Leap to a note outside the chord, then a step to a chord tone
effect_or_use: Accented. The strongest type for expression: the dissonance has the accent and the chord tone comes late

movement: Step to a note outside the chord, leap to a second such note, step to a chord tone
effect_or_use: Two notes around the chord tone

movement: One note stays while the chords change
effect_or_use: Usually the tonic or the dominant in the lowest voice. The chords above it become dissonant against it

movement: The bass has a note that is not in the chord above it
effect_or_use: The most elementary form of pandiatonic harmony
example: Stravinsky; the Elektra chord of Strauss

movement: A note outside the key that moves by a semitone
effect_or_use: More frequent from the Romantic period on

movement: A note outside the chord stays to the subsequent change of harmony
effect_or_use: It makes a seventh chord or an extended chord. Nadeau: each such note "became frozen into the chordal mass"; ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth chords became normal

movement: A major second or ninth above the root of a triad, with the third in the chord
effect_or_use: Added notes are "more intense substitutes for traditional chords"

movement: A perfect fourth above the root of a triad, with the third in the chord
A major or minor sixth above the root of a triad
effect_or_use: The chord with a sixth and a ninth is "not a tense chord requiring resolution"

movement: The major third and the minor third of one root, an octave or more apart
effect_or_use: Usually the minor third is above the major third

movement: All seven notes of a scale are free to sound together. No rules of resolution
effect_or_use: Triads with an added sixth, seventh, or second are the most frequent chords. A strong sense of key, "with a distinct preference for major keys"
example: Stravinsky, Symphony of Psalms III. Copland, Appalachian Spring. Prokofiev, start of Piano Concerto No. 3

movement: Two or more modes on one tonic at the same time or in sequence. Example: the Phrygian mode and the Lydian mode on C give all twelve notes
effect_or_use: Each chromatic note is a member of a mode on the tonic (Bartók: a "diatonic ingredient"). The key centre stays
example: Bartók, Mikrokosmos No. 80. Bartók, Harvard lectures (1943)

movement: A chord of many notes (to all twelve) that has only two interval types between adjacent notes
effect_or_use: Lutosławski keeps the dense chords for climaxes. They are not clusters: each chord has its own colour
example: Lutosławski, Musique funèbre (tritones and semitones); Symphony No. 2 (major seconds and fourths)
